extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent attorneys, and students/practitioners of UK patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the amount of invention required to support a patent and on who may be a patentee under UK law, illustrated by judicial authorities and examples. Covers when applications of known articles/processes are patentable, the role of novelty/ingenuity, and applicant eligibility rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of known parts may be patentable if combination is new and produces new result
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a machine each part of which was in use before may be good if 'the combination of different parts is new and a new result is produced, because there is novelty in the combination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the union has been 'effected in a mode unknown before, as applied in any degree to similar purposes,' that may be good ground for a patent. (Brunton v. Hawthorn, cited)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere substitution or reduction in number without novel mode is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A man cannot be entitled to a patent for uniting two things instead of three, where that union is effected in a mode well known and long practised for a similar purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: replacing three pieces with two by well-known means is not inventive (Brunton v. Hawthorn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Small dimensional adjustments or arranging known parts at particular distances are not inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of a particular distance between known parts (e.g., placing parts within two and a half inches) does not, where distances had varied previously and lesser reaches existed in analogous machines, constitute such an invention as would support a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adopting the particular spacing merely prevents the earlier patentee from using his invention with the old machine, the patent will be invalid (Kay v. Marshall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a known machine in a known manner to obtain an advantage is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery that a particular advantage may be obtained by using a known machine in a known manner is not a patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Tetley v. Easton; embossing/calendering example (patterned roller with bowl at unequal speeds) — amounted to showing how to use existing machine more beneficially, not patentable (Ralston v. Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of analogous elements (e.g., slide for hinge) is not patentable when previously known
rubrics_metrics.description: The substitution of a slide for a hinge, or application of a sliding door to a cylindrical lamp, was held not patentable when sliding doors had been previously fitted to cylindrical lamps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Parket v. Stevent and affirmed cases where mere substitution of analogous components failed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of old devices by obvious means requiring only ordinary skill is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of old locking apparatus with old actuating apparatus for railway signals did not display sufficient amount of invention where the combination was effected by obvious means and did not call for more than ordinary mechanical skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sarlin v. The Gloucester Waggon Company; similar holdings in Williams v. Ayer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical usefulness or commercial success alone does not establish patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding proof of practical usefulness and of a large sale, an alleged improvement (e.g., bat handles with grooves and enlarged ends) was held not to be good subject-matter for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success is relevant but cannot overcome lack of novelty/ingenuity (Slade v. Feltham).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of a known chemical or material to a known purpose is not patentable absent new process or apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere application of a known chemical or material (e.g., sulphides of calcium, solid naphthaline in stick form) to effects already achieved by known means is not proper subject-matter for a patent if no new apparatus or process is devised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification shows how the known material is to be used in a particular way, that disclosure may overcome the objection (Patterson v. Gas Light & Coke Co.; Hills v. London Gas Light Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents for 'applications' (applying known articles/processes) are disfavoured
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents for inventions referring to the application of an existing article to a purpose for which other similar articles have previously been used, or the application of a well-known process to produce a well-known article, are not favoured by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule: 'the mere application of the old machinery in the old manner to an analogous substance ... cannot be the subject of a patent.' (Brook v. Aston; Lord Campbell)

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of analogy / 'affinity' between purposes determines patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is one of degree: whether the amount of affinity or similarity between the two purposes is such that they are substantially the same; this determines whether the invention is sufficiently meritorious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the use or application is merely analogous the patent cannot be granted; if it is sufficiently out of the beaten track the patent may be upheld (Harwood; Lister v. Norton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-by-case, non-scientific evaluation of 'amount of invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions are not precise or scientific; it is impracticable to frame scientific propositions on this point — every case must be decided on its peculiar merits and special circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial decisions are guides only; courts assess degree of inventiveness in context (Lister v. Norton commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use in analogous machines/fields can defeat patent for new application
rubrics_metrics.description: If similar contrivances have been employed previously (even in another field), applying them to a cognate machine will not be novel unless some ingenuity is displayed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use of crushing rollers in cocoa-nut husk separation anticipated by hemp treatment; guides in drilling machines; C-springs for carriage fronts anticipated by earlier use (Hyde v. Trent; Jettiell; Hill v. Morgan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a new material to produce a known article is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of a new material (e.g., Russian tops wool) to produce a known article is not the subject of a patent if nothing inventive in method or apparatus is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: 'The use of a new material to produce a known article is not the subject of a patent.' (Thompson v. James etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: A second patent for improvement on an existing patented invention is permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: A second patent for an improvement on an invention which is the subject of a previous patent (even if afterwards assigned to the second patentee) is not void as contrary to public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An improved invention later patented by the same or another is not thrown open to the world merely because it improves the earlier patented article (Lister v. Leather; Thomson v. Batty; Edison & Swan Co. v. Holland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness requirement for successive applications of same thing
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a patent for a certain application of a given (non-new) thing will not vitiate a subsequent patent for another application of the same thing, provided the two applications are perfectly distinct and the second is not in any way comprised in the first specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Newton v. Vaucher — different applications of soft metal were essentially different and Newton's patent was novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main test: does the new application require thought/study beyond natural suggestion?
rubrics_metrics.description: One main consideration is whether the new application lies so much out of the track of former use as not naturally to suggest itself, but to require some application of thought and study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it would not naturally suggest itself to a person turning his mind to the subject, that supports patentability (Penn v. Libby).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical inventions judged differently from mechanical ones — analogy matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications of chemical novelties may be treated differently from purely mechanical analogies; the fields' different natures affect whether an application is patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrast: applying caustic alkalies in flour manufacture was held non-patentable by analogy cases, but obtaining paraffine oil from bituminous coal (Yenning v. Arnott) was upheld — 'inventions in mechanics are as widely different from inventions in economical chemistry' (Stuart, J.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification showing how to apply a known substance can sustain a patent claim
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee shows how a known substance (e.g., hydrated oxides of iron) is to be used in a particular way, an objection that it is merely the use of a known property may fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court of Exchequer held that mere claim to use might be insufficient, but practical disclosure of method can render it patentable (Hills v. London Gas Light Co.; compare Ormson v. Clarke).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may apply for a patent (statutory eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute (Patents Act 1883 s.4) any person, whether a British subject or not, may make application for a patent; two or more persons may make a joint application and a patent may be granted to them jointly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must include the person(s) claiming to be the true and first inventor; the application must contain a declaration to that effect (Patents Act s.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office will not entertain application unless true and first inventor is an applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: No application will be entertained unless the person(s) claiming to be the true and first inventor are applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-inventors may join, but the Patent Office insists the inventor be an applicant (citing Carfrae v. Glendinning and statutory rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-inventors may join applications and become joint patentees
rubrics_metrics.description: Other persons who are non-inventors may join in the application, and in that case the patent will be issued to all the applicants, who will be joint patentees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents Act (1885) s.5 allows such arrangements; practical for assignments/trusts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporations and inventors can jointly apply; 'person' includes bodies corporate
rubrics_metrics.description: Although no specific form existed enabling an inventor and an incorporated company to apply jointly, this may be done; by sect.117 of the Act of 1888 'person' includes a body corporate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint applications between natural persons and corporations are permissible in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importers/first introducers can be patentees if invention is new in England
rubrics_metrics.description: Importing an invention from a foreign country and being first to bring it into England may qualify one for a patent, provided the invention is new and useful in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-standing practice permits an importer to obtain a patent if the invention is new in England (Edgebery v. Stevens; Carpenter v. Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Residency requirement for communication patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Form A of the Patents Rules (1890) and later practice render it necessary that the applicant for a 'communication patent' must be resident in the United Kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although aliens may be grantees and patents have been granted to aliens, specific procedural forms limit communication patents to residents (In re Wirth's Patent; Form A).
